messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Vignette:
Amara Osei was twenty-four years old when the IED detonated beneath the lead Humvee of her convoy. She was the battalion surgeon, riding three vehicles back, and the blast threw her against the armored door before the ringing in her ears gave way to screams. She scrambled out into smoke and dust, found the driver with a femoral bleed, and worked her hands into the warm, wet cavity of his thigh while the rotor blades of the medevac helicopter pounded overhead. That sound—the *thwump-thwump-thwump*—would later lodge itself in her chest like a second heart. The texture of the driver’s torn uniform, a gritty nylon webbing slick with blood and dirt, pressed into her palms for what felt like hours. She could not remember the words she said to him, only the feel of that fabric, the shock of each new explosion from mortar rounds still landing a few hundred meters away, and the absolute terror that she was going to die before she could finish the tourniquet. He survived. She did not.

Now, a year later, Amara was a trauma surgeon at a Level I center in Chicago, and the war had followed her into the sterile hallways. When she walked into the operating room, the first thing she did was locate every exit, every alternate route, every corner where she might have to run. She checked the doors, the crash cart, the oxygen tanks—scanning for anything that might become a threat. Her residents noticed that she always chose the stool that put her back to the wall, that she never let anyone stand behind her. They thought it was a quirk of habit. She knew it was the only way she could breathe.

The triggers came without warning, and they came as feelings, not memories. A patient’s wound packing—the wet, gritty texture of gauze against a raw wound—could send a flash of pure terror through her chest before she had even registered why. Her hands would freeze for a split second, and then she would force them to move again, because the patient was bleeding out and there was no time. Helicopter sounds were worse. Whenever a medical helicopter landed on the roof pad, the ceiling shook with a low, familiar thrum, and Amara would feel herself back in that Humvee, the blast wave still reverberating through her bones. She never knew when it would hit. An explosion on the news, a car backfiring, a dropped metal tray in the cafeteria—any of them could drop her into the same state of animal terror she had felt that day, and she could not find the words to explain it. When her attending once asked why she had flinched at a slammed door, she said she was tired. She did not know how to describe the way the memory did not have a story; it was just the feeling of dying, without context, without language.

The avoidance leaked into every part of her life. Before she entered any new room—a conference hall, a restaurant, a friend’s apartment—she had to plan her escape route. She would walk the perimeter, note the exits, the windows, the likelihood of a clear path to the door. She could not sit at a table unless her back was against a wall, because otherwise she felt the exposed vulnerability of her spine, and the scanning never stopped. Her social life shriveled. She stopped accepting dinner invitations from colleagues because she could not explain why she needed to sit in a particular chair, or why she flinched at the sound of the kitchen door swinging shut. On the rare occasions she went out, she was always the one scanning the crowd, checking the exits, braced for a threat that never materialized but that felt absolutely real.

It was a three-week stretch of sleepless nights and daytime intrusive flashes that finally pushed her into the clinic. A trauma patient had arrived with a tourniquet on his leg, and the sight of the blood-soaked fabric had sent her into such a dissociated episode that she dropped a scalpel. The attending sent her home. That evening, she tried to write down what happened, to make sense of it, but the words would not come. The terror was there, in her body, but it had no story. She had no language for what she was feeling, only the certainty that she could not keep living like this. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the way they owned her—how a texture or a sound could remake the world into a battlefield at any moment. She came to the clinic hoping, though she could not say it out loud, that someone might help her find a story for the terror, so that it would not always remain a wordless, ambushing thing.
